pointers.sentence: `DetailView` inherits from `SingleObjectTemplateResponseMixin` and `BaseDetailView`, and has no body beyond a docstring (`django/views/generic/detail.py:DetailView`).

Every generic view that renders a template is assembled so, from two halves, except `TemplateView`, which is written in one piece: its bases are two mixins and `View`, and its `get` is its own (`django/views/generic/base.py:TemplateView`).

`BaseDetailView.get` finds the object and builds the context, and then calls `render_to_response`, a method that neither it nor any of its bases declares, so a subclass has to supply it (`django/views/generic/detail.py:BaseDetailView`).
And it lays the view's `extra_context` over the top, when that attribute is not `None` (`django/views/generic/base.py:ContextMixin.get_context_data`).

The other mixins of `django/views/generic/` that declare a `get_context_data`, `SingleObjectMixin`, `MultipleObjectMixin` and `FormMixin`, keep to one convention: each adds what it contributes, lets a keyword argument it received, but for `MultipleObjectMixin`'s `object_list`, take the place of its own value of the same name, and passes the result to `super().get_context_data`.

It calls `get_template_names`, and gives the result to `response_class`, which is `TemplateResponse` unless set otherwise, with the request, the context, and the view's `template_engine` and `content_type` (`django/views/generic/base.py:TemplateResponseMixin`).

`TemplateView` is the two mixins and `View` with a short `get` between them: the keyword arguments from the path go to `get_context_data`, and the context goes to `render_to_response` (`django/views/generic/base.py:TemplateView`).
`RedirectView` shares a module with `TemplateView` but none of its mixins: it is `View` with a `get` that redirects (`django/views/generic/base.py:RedirectView`).
If `query_string` is true, the request's query string is added to whatever was found (`django/views/generic/base.py:RedirectView.get_redirect_url`).

A target holding an escaped character must double the sign, `%%20` for `%20`: written as it would be sent, the escape makes `get_redirect_url` raise a `ValueError` or a `TypeError`, or changes the URL (`docs/ref/class-based-views/base.txt`, `django/views/generic/base.py:RedirectView.get_redirect_url`).

With it true, the response takes its class's other status, a 308 in place of a 301 and a 307 in place of a 302, which ask the client to repeat the request at the new address with its method and body (`django/http/response.py:HttpResponseRedirectBase.__init__`).
When there is no target `get` answers with a 410, `HttpResponseGone`, and logs a warning (`django/views/generic/base.py:RedirectView.get`).
So a `RedirectView` redirects a `"POST"` or a `"DELETE"` as readily as a `"GET"`, and with the status a `"GET"` would get (`django/views/generic/base.py:RedirectView.post`).

Before it, a `RedirectView`'s redirect was a 301 or a 302, chosen by `permanent` alone, though the redirect classes had taken a `preserve_request` argument since 5.2; the view now passes its attribute to them (`docs/releases/6.1.txt`, `docs/releases/5.2.txt`).
